meta.subject: Physics
chapterTopics: 1.1 Physical Quantities (base, derived, SI units, prefixes, scalar, vector)
meta.purpose: Accuracy benchmark for theory marking points, scores, and model-answer cards

questions.question: Define base quantity and give three examples. (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: Base quantity cannot be defined/derived from other physical quantities
Any three valid examples (e.g. length, mass, time, current, temperature, luminous intensity, amount of substance)

trials.studentAnswer: A base quantity is a physical quantity that cannot be derived from other physical quantities. Examples are length, mass and time.
Length, mass and time are base quantities.

questions.question: Define derived quantity and give two examples. (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: Derived quantity is obtained from combinations of base quantities by multiplication and/or division
Two valid examples (e.g. speed, density, force, area, volume, acceleration)

trials.studentAnswer: A derived quantity is a physical quantity that is derived from base quantities by multiplication or division. Examples are speed and density.
Speed and force are derived quantities.
Derived quantity is the same as base quantity like mass.

questions.question: What is meant by a physical quantity? (1 mark)
expectedMarkingPoints: A quantity that can be measured (and stated with magnitude and unit)

trials.studentAnswer: A physical quantity is a quantity that can be measured.
idk

questions.question: State the SI units for mass and electric current. (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: Mass: kilogram (kg)
Electric current: ampere (A)

trials.studentAnswer: Mass is measured in kilogram, kg. Electric current is measured in ampere, A.
Mass is in kg.
Mass is in grams and current is in volts.

questions.question: List three base quantities and their SI units. (3 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: One correct base quantity with SI unit
Second correct base quantity with SI unit
Third correct base quantity with SI unit

trials.studentAnswer: Length — metre (m); Mass — kilogram (kg); Time — second (s).
Length — metre. Mass — kilogram.
Speed — m/s; Force — N; Energy — J.

questions.question: Differentiate between a scalar quantity and a vector quantity. (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: Scalar has magnitude only
Vector has magnitude and direction

trials.studentAnswer: A scalar quantity has magnitude only while a vector quantity has both magnitude and direction.
Vector has magnitude and direction.

questions.question: State two examples of scalar quantities. (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: One valid scalar example (e.g. mass, time, distance, speed, energy, temperature)
Second valid scalar example

trials.studentAnswer: Mass and time.
Mass.
Force and velocity.

questions.question: State two examples of vector quantities. (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: One valid vector example (e.g. displacement, velocity, force, acceleration, weight, momentum)
Second valid vector example

trials.studentAnswer: Force and velocity.
Force.
Mass and energy.

questions.question: Explain the difference between distance and displacement. (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: Distance is the total length of path travelled (scalar)
Displacement is the shortest length from initial to final position in a stated direction (vector)

trials.studentAnswer: Distance is the total length of the path travelled and is a scalar. Displacement is the shortest distance from start to end point in a given direction and is a vector.
Displacement has direction but distance does not.
Distance and displacement are the same thing.

questions.question: Differentiate between speed and velocity. (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: Speed is rate of change of distance (scalar / magnitude only)
Velocity is rate of change of displacement (vector / has direction)

trials.studentAnswer: Speed is the rate of change of distance and is a scalar quantity. Velocity is the rate of change of displacement and is a vector quantity.
Velocity has direction but speed does not.
asdf

questions.question: Density is a derived quantity. Express density in terms of base quantities and state its SI unit in base units. (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: Density = mass / volume (or mass / length³)
SI base unit: kg m⁻³

trials.studentAnswer: Density equals mass divided by volume, so in base quantities it is mass per length cubed. Its SI unit is kg m⁻³.
Density = mass / volume.
Density unit is g/cm³ only.

questions.question: Show that the SI unit of acceleration can be written as m s⁻² in terms of base units. (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: Acceleration = change in velocity / time (or displacement/time²)
Unit becomes m s⁻¹ / s = m s⁻²

trials.studentAnswer: Acceleration is change of velocity divided by time. Velocity unit is m s⁻¹, so acceleration unit is m s⁻¹ divided by s, which is m s⁻².
Acceleration unit is m/s².
Acceleration unit is m/s.

questions.question: State the values of the prefixes milli and kilo in powers of ten. (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: milli = 10⁻³
kilo = 10³

trials.studentAnswer: Milli means 10⁻³ and kilo means 10³.
Kilo is 1000 or 10³.
Milli is 10⁶ and kilo is 10⁻³.

questions.question: Convert 5.0 km to metres and 250 ms to seconds. (2 marks)

trials.studentAnswer: 5 km = 5 m and 250 ms = 250 s.

questions.question: Express 0.00045 in scientific notation. (1 mark)
Explain why a physical quantity must be stated with a magnitude and a unit. (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: Magnitude gives the numerical value of the measurement
Unit tells the standard used so the value is meaningful / comparable

trials.studentAnswer: The magnitude gives the numerical value of the quantity. The unit shows the standard of measurement so that the value has clear meaning and can be compared.
Without a unit we do not know what the number means.
ok

questions.question: State one difference between mass and weight. (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: Mass is amount of matter / scalar / SI unit kg
Weight is gravitational force / vector / SI unit N (or depends on gravity)

trials.studentAnswer: Mass is the amount of matter in a body and is a scalar measured in kg. Weight is the gravitational force acting on the body and is a vector measured in newtons.
Weight is a force but mass is not.
Mass and weight are the same and both use kg.

questions.question: Force has SI unit newton (N). Express the newton in base SI units. (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: F = ma (or force related to mass × acceleration)
1 N = kg m s⁻²

trials.studentAnswer: From F = ma, newton is kilogram times metre per second squared, so 1 N = kg m s⁻².
Newton is kg m s⁻².
Newton is the same as kg.

questions.question: In a scientific investigation, state the meaning of manipulated variable, responding variable and fixed variable. (3 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: Manipulated (independent) variable is changed by the investigator
Responding (dependent) variable is measured / changes due to manipulation
Fixed (controlled) variable is kept constant

trials.studentAnswer: Manipulated variable is the variable that is deliberately changed. Responding variable is the variable that is measured. Fixed variable is kept constant throughout the experiment.
Manipulated variable is changed by us. Responding variable is measured.
All variables must change together.

questions.question: Differentiate between an inference and a hypothesis in a scientific investigation. (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: Inference is an early explanation based on observation
Hypothesis is a testable statement relating manipulated and responding variables

trials.studentAnswer: An inference is a preliminary explanation made from observations. A hypothesis is a testable statement that relates the manipulated variable to the responding variable.
A hypothesis can be tested in an experiment.

questions.question: A graph of y against x is a straight line through the origin. State the relationship between y and x and write the equation relating them. (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: y is directly proportional to x (y ∝ x)
y = mx (or y = kx)

trials.studentAnswer: y is directly proportional to x. The equation is y = mx where m is the gradient.
y is directly proportional to x.
y is inversely proportional to x so y = m/x.

questions.question: A graph of y against 1/x is a straight line through the origin. State the relationship between y and x. (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: y is directly proportional to 1/x (or y ∝ 1/x)
Therefore y is inversely proportional to x

trials.studentAnswer: y is directly proportional to 1/x, so y is inversely proportional to x.
y is inversely proportional to x.
y does not depend on x.

questions.question: Explain how to determine the gradient of a straight-line graph from plotted points. (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: Choose two points on the line and find Δy and Δx (from a large triangle)
Gradient = Δy / Δx (rise over run)

trials.studentAnswer: Draw a large triangle on the straight line. Measure the change in y and the change in x. Gradient equals Δy divided by Δx.
Gradient is rise over run, Δy/Δx.
Gradient is always the intercept on the y-axis.

questions.question: State what the y-intercept of a graph of y against x represents in the equation y = mx + c. (1 mark)
expectedMarkingPoints: The value of y when x = 0 (constant c)

trials.studentAnswer: The y-intercept is the value of y when x is zero, which is constant c.
It is the gradient of the graph.

questions.question: In an experiment to investigate the period of a simple pendulum, identify one suitable manipulated variable, one responding variable and one fixed variable. (3 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: Manipulated: length of pendulum (or angle / mass if justified by design)
Responding: period / time for oscillations
Fixed: mass of bob / amplitude / length (whichever not manipulated)

trials.studentAnswer: Manipulated variable: length of the pendulum. Responding variable: period of oscillation. Fixed variable: mass of the bob.
Manipulated variable is length. Responding variable is period.
Everything must be changed at once to get better results.

questions.question: Explain the difference between accuracy and precision in measurements, and state why both are important in scientific investigations. (3 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: Accuracy: closeness of a measurement to the true/accepted value
Precision: closeness of repeated measurements to each other
Importance: accuracy gives correct results; precision gives reliable/consistent results

trials.studentAnswer: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value. Precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other. Both are important because accuracy ensures correct results and precision ensures reliable consistent results.
Accuracy means getting the correct answer. Precision means repeating the same result.

questions.question: Express the SI units of area and volume in base units. (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: Area: m²
Volume: m³

trials.studentAnswer: Area is m² and volume is m³.
Area is metre squared.
Area is m and volume is m².

questions.question: Pressure is force per unit area. Express the SI unit of pressure (pascal) in base units. (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: P = F/A with F in N and A in m²
1 Pa = N m⁻² = kg m⁻¹ s⁻²

trials.studentAnswer: Pressure = force / area. Since 1 N = kg m s⁻², one pascal is N m⁻² which equals kg m⁻¹ s⁻².
Pascal is N/m².
Pressure unit is only N.

questions.question: In a simple pendulum experiment, a graph of T² against length l is a straight line through the origin. What conclusion can be made about the relationship between T² and l? (2 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: T² is directly proportional to l
T² = kl (or period squared increases linearly with length)

trials.studentAnswer: T² is directly proportional to the length l. The relationship can be written as T² = kl where k is the gradient.
T² is directly proportional to l.
T does not depend on length.

questions.question: Define scalar quantity and vector quantity, and state why it is important to distinguish between them in measurements involving motion. (3 marks)
expectedMarkingPoints: Scalar: magnitude only
Vector: magnitude and direction
Importance: direction affects displacement/velocity/acceleration analysis in motion

trials.studentAnswer: A scalar quantity has magnitude only. A vector quantity has magnitude and direction. Distinguishing them is important because direction is needed to describe displacement and velocity correctly in motion.
Scalar has magnitude only. Vector has magnitude and direction.
